item.title: What I still had to do when AI built the app
item.description:
“Yeah, yeah, it works. Now save it. Oops.”

That was me trying the QR-code app in my NSLondon demo. It generated codes from text and links, so I was pleased with it. Then I tried to save one and found a bug.

I could copy the stack trace, or even better, take a screenshot because I’m lazy. I gave the agent the screenshot and suggested checking the sandbox. It found a missing entitlement, corrected it, and saving worked too.

item.title: Antescher: How Ant Attack Works
item.description: My Spectrum turned up late. Italy ran behind on home computers, so by the time one arrived in our house the machine was past its prime everywhere else, and the tapes we had were older still. I was a kid at school, which is exactly the right age not to know or care that you are late to something. Every game took minutes to load off cassette and I loved all of them indiscriminately.

item.title: A Morning Reset at Build with AI at Imperial College
item.description:
I only made it to the morning of Build with AI at Imperial College London on Saturday, March 14, 2026. It was enough to make the trip worth it.

GDG London and Women Techmakers held the event at the Blackett Laboratory. It did not feel like a day spent selling AI. People shared what they had learned, compared notes and spoke plainly about where the technology might be heading.

item.title: How I (Almost) Implemented a Production App in a Weekend
item.description:
Shameless plug: if you want better focus and sleep, download Neurona first, then come back for the build story.

I wanted a simple weekend experiment, specifically to try the Ralph Wiggum technique from Geoffrey Huntley’s original article, Ralph Wiggum as a “software engineer”. Instead, I got a very honest lesson in modern AI development: getting a prototype is fast, shipping a real app is still work.

item.title: Weekend Hack: Letting Ollama Sift 1,000 iOS Blogs for AI Gems
item.description:
Over the last year I’ve had the itch to build again. AI has made it easier to ship small things and use each one to push a longer plan forward: move from mobile expert, through mobile and AI, towards understanding AI as a product, not only the models.

The long game

I want to learn how people are actually using AI in mobile development. This weekend’s question was simple: who is writing about it in the iOS world?

item.title: Where Alan Turing Walked: Google DevFest at the National Museum of Computing
item.description:
Google DevFest took place inside the National Museum of Computing at Bletchley Park. Walking past codebreaking rooms and wartime machines on the way to talks about AI made the history unusually hard to ignore. Alan Turing worked at Bletchley Park during the Second World War, and later proposed the test that still bears his name.

GDG Bletchley mixed hands-on sessions with talks and left enough room for hallway conversations among the museum’s working restorations.

item.title: Demystifying AI Coding Agents in Swift
item.description:
The small loop behind an agent

AI coding agents can look opaque. You type a request and they search files, write code, refactor functions and decide what to do next.

The basic mechanism is much smaller than the behaviour it produces.

I tend to understand things by building them, so after reading Amp’s article “How to Build an Agent”, I tried the same idea in Swift.

The result is Nimbo, a small coding agent that can list directories, read files and edit code. Its core is a loop, a few tools and a language model with opinions.

item.title: AI-Accelerated Mobile Development at Londroid
item.description:
The talk

At Londroid at NewDay on 29 May 2025, I spoke to Android developers about using AI in solo and small-team workflows. I opened with a question: what if a one-person team could deliver like a studio? The rest of the talk looked at what changes when AI becomes part of the build chain instead of an IDE novelty.
